hints: Start by looking for the repeating pattern - find the dark vertical Z-lines and compare the very light areas next to them with the darker areas in the middle of each sarcomere.
Remember where each filament type is anchored - thin filaments attach to the Z-line and extend inward, while thick filaments stay centred on the M-line in the middle.
Think about overlap - where only one filament type exists the image looks paler, and where thin and thick filaments overlap the image looks darker.
walkthrough:
Read the Striations Like a Map**
You are looking at several sarcomeres side by side. The dark vertical lines are Z-lines, the boundaries of each sarcomere. Next to them is a light band because only thin filaments are there. In the centre of each sarcomere is the thick filament bundle.

Place P, Q and R by Filament Content**
P - actin only - goes to the light I-band right beside a Z-line. Q - myosin only - goes to the paler H-zone in the very centre around the M-line where thin filaments do not reach. R - both actin and myosin - goes to the darker region of the A-band where thin and thick filaments overlap.
Final answer: P to light area at Z-line (I-band, actin only); Q to paler central area at M-line (H-zone, myosin only); R to darker overlap area (A-band, actin and myosin).

hints: Think about the resting muscle first - what must be prevented so myosin cannot constantly grab actin?
Recall which of the two proteins actually covers the binding site and which one acts as the calcium sensor.
Follow the calcium signal - what ion is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and what protein does it bind to?
Link shape change to movement - how does a change in one protein physically uncover the binding site for the myosin head?
walkthrough:
The Resting Block**
Think of tropomyosin as a long thread lying along the actin filament. At rest it sits directly over the myosin-binding sites on actin, so myosin heads cannot attach. This prevents unwanted contraction.

Calcium Switches Contraction On**
When an impulse arrives, $Ca^{2+}$ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to troponin, which is attached to tropomyosin. Troponin changes shape and pulls tropomyosin aside.

Exposing Sites for Crossbridges**
With tropomyosin moved, the binding sites on actin are exposed. Myosin heads can now bind to actin and form crossbridges, allowing the sliding filament power stroke to occur.

Final answer: At rest tropomyosin covers myosin-binding sites on actin; $Ca^{2+}$ binds to troponin causing troponin to change shape, moving tropomyosin away to expose binding sites so myosin heads bind and form crossbridges.

hints: Think about what a contracting muscle constantly uses up - what energy molecule and what fuel stores power crossbridge cycling and ion pumping?
Think about what builds up or runs out during prolonged anaerobic respiration and repeated stimulation.
walkthrough:
Running Out of Supplies**
Contraction needs continuous ATP for myosin head movement and for pumping $Ca^{2+}$ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. ATP is made using glucose, glycogen, creatine phosphate and oxygen. After long activity these fall, so less ATP and less $Ca^{2+}$ release means fewer crossbridges form and cycle more slowly.

Build-up of Waste**
If oxygen runs low, muscle respires anaerobically and lactate accumulates. This lowers pH and reduces enzyme and protein function, so contraction becomes less efficient - this is fatigue.

Final answer: Any two from: less $Ca^{2+}$ for troponin activation; less ATP for crossbridge detachment and power stroke; less glucose / glycogen / creatine phosphate / oxygen for aerobic respiration; build-up of lactate / lactic acid lowering pH and inhibiting enzymes.
